questions.question: Which generation produces spores in archegoniates ?
questions.solution_html:
• Sporophyte (Dominant Phase)
  • The palm like plant body is the diploid sporophyte which is dioecious,
  • Male Plant -Produces a large cone called a microsporangiate strobilus which contains microsporophylls
  • bearing microsporangia.
  • Female Plant-Does not form a true cone (unlike many gymnosperms) and bears megasporophylls arranged
  • in a rosette at the apex. Each megasporophyll carries ovules (megasporangia) on its margins.

• Formation of Gametophytes
  • (A) Male Gametophyte Development
  • Inside microsporangia, microspore mother cells undergo meiosis → form haploid microspores (pollen
  • grains). Each pollen grain develops into a male gametophyte, consisting of prothallial cells and
  • generative cell which forms two large, motile sperm (antherozoids)
  • (B) Female Gametophyte Development
  • Inside the ovule, a megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis and forms 4 megaspores (only one
  • functional).
  • The functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte (haploid endosperm).

questions.question: Explain progressive dominance and independence of the sporophyte in archegoniates
questions.solution_html:
• Explain progressive dominance and independence of the sporophyte in archegoniates.
  • Ans: The progressive dominance and independence of the sporophyte is a fundamental evolutionary trend
  • in archegoniates (bryophytes, pteridophytes, and gymnosperms). This involves a shift from a short-lived,
  • dependent sporophyte in bryophytes to a dominant, free-living sporophyte in vascular plants, allowing for
  • better colonization of land.
  • Dependent Sporophyte in Bryophytes -In bryophytes (liverworts and mosses), the sporophyte
  • is physically attached to the gametophyte and relies on it entirely or partially for nutrition and water
  • Transition towards Independence in hornworts- This group shows a crucial intermediate step where the
  • sporophyte has an intercalary meristem (allowing continuous growth) and is photosynthetic.
  • Progressive Dominance & Independence in Pteridophytes- The sporophyte is perennial and showing
  • unlimited growth and completely independent of the gametophyte
  • Ultimate Dominance in Gymnosperms and Angiosperms- The gametophyte is extremely reduced (e.g.,
  • pollen grains and embryo sac) and relies entirely on the sporophyte for survival and the dominant
  • sporophyte is perfectly adapted to dry environments

• Give a detailed account of the mature antheridium of Anthoceros
  • A mature antheridium of Anthoceros is a club-shaped or pouch-like male reproductive organ developed
  • dorsally inside an enclosed, mucilage-filled antheridial chamber. It consists of a multicellular stalk and a
  • main body, enveloped by a single-layered sterile jacket, which changes from green to bright red or orange at
  • maturity, and it contains numerous small, unicellular, biflagellate, curved antherozoids.

questions.question: Give an account on PPG system of classification.
questions.solution_html:
• Give an account on PPG system of classification.
  • The Pteridophyte Phylogeny Group (PPG) classification (2016), is a modern, community-derived,
  • molecular-based taxonomic system for extant ferns and lycophytes. It organizes these plants based on
  • monophyletic relationships, recognizing two distinct classes: Lycopodiopsida (Lycophytes like club mosses,
  • spike mosses,etc.) and Polypodiopsida (horsetails, ferns,etc), covering 51 families and over 11,900 species.
  • It focuses only on extant (living) plants

questions.question: Describe the structure and distinctive features of the megasporophyll of Cycas. [5x6 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the structure and distinctive features of the megasporophyll of Cycas.
  • Ans: Megasporophylls are loosely arranged on the crown of the stem, in female Cycas plants , not
  • in a compact strobilus like in male Cycas.The megasporophyll of Cycas is a leaf-like, brownish structure
  • that serves as the female reproductive organ, bearing ovules on its margins . It is differentiated into a leafy,
  • serrated upper lamina, a central ovule-bearing stalk that bears 1-6 pairs (or up to 12) of large, sessile ovules
  • (megasporangia), and a lower petiole, arranged in a crown-like rosette. Unlike male cones, female
  • megasporophylls are loosely arranged in a crown on the crown of the stem, not in a compact strobilus.
  • The ovules are orthotropous (straight), unitegmic (single integument), and the largest in the plant kingdom.
  • The entire megasporophyll is typically covered in yellow or brown hairs (tomentum). The megasporophyll
  • is highly variable between species, often with the upper part being narrow and dissected.

questions.question: With the help of labelled diagram, explain the structure of strobilus in Selaginella.
questions.solution_html:
• With the help of labelled diagram, explain the structure of strobilus in Selaginella.
  • The genus Selaginella, is a heterosporous vascular plant that produces two distinct types of spores
  • (microspores and megaspores). These spores are housed within specialized sporangia located at the tips of
  • aerial branches, forming a compact, conical structure known as the strobilus or cone. The strobilus
  • represents a significant step in the evolution of heterospory and the seed habit, concentrating the
  • reproductive organs at the apex for efficient spore dispersal.
